name: The Recursive I Ching — a book you cast
description: A book with a fixed beginning and a fixed end, and a middle that does not exist until you cast it. Cast how you are; walk the changing lines toward Hexagram 1, the Creative; learn one hexagram at a time; write your own transitions; save it as your own grammar; print it if you like. A casting, not a prediction.

sections.Text:
You are about to read a book that does not exist yet. It has a beginning, which is this page, and it has an end, which is Hexagram 1 — the Creative, six unbroken lines, the one every path in this book arrives at. Between the two there is nothing until you cast.

Here is how it works. You cast six lines — three coins, or the yarrow stalks if you have the patience — and the hexagram that comes up is where you are standing. Not who you are. Where you are, today, in the weather you woke up in. From there the book moves one line at a time. A line changes, and the hexagram becomes another hexagram, and the text the tradition wrote for that exact line — some three thousand years ago, for exactly this change — is the page that carries you across. Then another line. Then another. You will pass through hexagrams you would never have chosen, and that is the point; a book you choose your way through is a book you already knew.

Every hexagram is a meeting of two things from a list of eight: heaven, earth, thunder, wind, water, fire, mountain, lake. Water over thunder. Mountain over fire. Earth over earth. You will meet water more than once on almost any path, and it will not be the same water — which is how anyone learns anything, by meeting it again from a different side. At each hexagram this book gives you what it knows: the old text, the image, what the two elements are doing to each other. Where the story for that hexagram has been written, you will find it. Where it hasn't, you will find an honest blank, and a place to write what happened to you there.

That place is the part of this book that matters most. Under every step there is a box that says *your transition*. Write in it. What you were carrying when that line changed. What the text made you think of. Nothing, if nothing came. When you reach the end you can save the whole walk — the hexagrams, the changing lines, your words — as a grammar of your own, and keep it, or print it, or hand it to someone. That copy will be the only one. Nobody else will ever cast this book the way you did.

Two honesties before you begin. First: one changing line turning one hexagram into another is exactly what the I Ching itself describes. A path of several changes, through hexagrams in between, is this project's own extension — held lightly, as a way of reading, not as scripture. Second: this is a casting, not a prediction. The coins do not know your future. They know how to interrupt you, and an interruption, met honestly, is most of what a book is for.

Others have made books this way. A Californian novelist consulted this very oracle for every turn of a novel and put the oracle inside the novel doing the same. An Italian laid tarot cards in a grid and read the stories along the rows. An Englishman published a book in a box, first and last chapters marked, the rest to be shuffled. This one is theirs and yours. Cast.

sections.Text:
Six unbroken lines. You have arrived at the one hexagram that is made of nothing but yang — heaven over heaven, the Creative, the thing that makes. Every path in this book ends here, and it is worth asking why, because it is not the answer you might expect.

It is not because heaven is the goal. In the received order of the I Ching this hexagram is not the end of the book; it is the *beginning* — the first page, the first thing named, before earth, before anything has happened. The book you have just cast runs the other way. You started wherever the coins put you, in the middle of things, in some weather, and walked backward through the changes to the place where the changes come from. You did not climb to the top. You walked back to the source.

And here is what the source turns out to be. Everything you passed through on the way — the water, the thunder, the mountain that would not move, the lake that showed you your face — was made of this and one other thing, the Receptive, six broken lines, the earth that takes what heaven gives and makes it into something. Two ingredients. Sixty-four meetings. Your whole path was those two, in different proportions, meeting each other again and again and calling it weather. There was never anything in the book but the Creative and the Receptive taking turns. There was never anything in you but the same.

The tradition has a word for the moment when the one who was walking notices that the walking and the ground and the walker were never separate. It is not a mystical word; it is closer to what happens when you recognise a face you had been looking at for some time without knowing you knew it. The thing that cast the coins is the thing the coins were describing. You were the weather. That is the recognition, and this book cannot give it to you; it can only walk you back to the place where it is most likely to happen and leave you there, at the first page, with six unbroken lines and nothing yet made.

So this is not an ending. The received book ends on Hexagram 64, *Before Completion* — the oldest book of changes closes on *not yet*. This one ends on Hexagram 1, which is where that one begins. Go back and cast again if you like; it will be a different book. Or don't. Take what you wrote in the boxes, save it, print it, give it to someone who is standing where you were standing when you started. That is what the Creative does with what it makes. It does not keep it.
